symptoms: sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet foods
visible holes or pits in teeth
guidance: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, floss daily, and limit sugary snacks and drinks. Use a fluoride mouthwash. If a cavity is present, see a dentist for filling. In early stages, fluoride treatments may reverse decay. Free dental care is available at government hospitals.
precautions: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste
Floss daily to remove plaque between teeth
Attend regular dental checkups every 6 months
Consider dental sealants for children's molars

symptoms: yellow or brown deposits on teeth
guidance: Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria that hardens into tartar if not removed. Brushing and flossing remove plaque; tartar requires professional scaling. Regular dental cleanings prevent gum disease and tooth decay. Use an electric toothbrush for better plaque removal.
precautions: Visit a dentist for scaling every 6–12 months

symptoms: gums may be shiny or puffy
guidance: Gingivitis is reversible with good oral hygiene. Brush gently, floss daily, and use an antibacterial mouthwash. If symptoms persist for more than 2 weeks, see a dentist. Professional cleaning may be needed. Untreated gingivitis can progress to periodontitis.
precautions: Brush gently but thoroughly twice a day
Floss daily to remove plaque from between teeth

symptoms: deep pockets between teeth and gums
guidance: Periodontitis requires professional treatment: scaling and root planing, antibiotics, or surgery in severe cases. It is a leading cause of tooth loss. Manage risk factors: smoking, diabetes, and poor hygiene. Free periodontal care is available at government dental colleges.
precautions: Treat gingivitis early – do not ignore bleeding gums
Quit smoking – a major risk factor
Get professional deep cleaning as advised

symptoms: swelling of the face, cheek, or jaw
guidance: This is a dental emergency. See a dentist immediately. Treatment: drainage of the abscess, root canal treatment, or extraction. Antibiotics may be prescribed. Do not delay – infection can spread to other parts of the body. Free emergency dental care is available.
precautions: Do not ignore severe tooth pain
Do not apply heat – use cold packs to reduce swelling
Maintain good oral hygiene to prevent future abscesses

symptoms: sometimes a fistula (pimple) on the gum
guidance: Caused by infection at the root tip. Treatment: root canal therapy (endodontic treatment) or extraction. Antibiotics may be given for acute infection. Early treatment saves the tooth. Free root canal treatment may be available at government dental colleges.
precautions: Do not ignore dull tooth pain
If you have a gum pimple, see a dentist
Get root canal treatment rather than extraction if possible

symptoms: pain that lasts longer than 30 seconds to cold/hot stimuli
guidance: Pulpitis is inflammation of the dental pulp. Reversible pulpitis may heal with a filling; irreversible pulpitis requires root canal treatment or extraction. See a dentist promptly. Avoid hot/cold extremes. Free care available.
precautions: Do not delay dental visit for tooth pain
Avoid very hot or cold foods if sensitive
If pain is severe at night, seek urgent care
Keep teeth clean to prevent further decay
If you grind your teeth, use a night guard

guidance: Small cracks may be repaired with bonding; larger cracks may need a crown; if the crack extends to the root, extraction may be needed. See a dentist immediately. Avoid chewing on hard foods. Do not ignore – can lead to infection.
precautions: Avoid chewing on hard objects (ice, bones, pens)
If you have a cracked tooth, do not chew on that side
Wear a mouthguard if you grind your teeth
Seek dental care early to save the tooth
If you have a sharp edge, cover with dental wax

guidance: Caused by acidic foods, drinks (citrus, soda), or acid reflux. Use a soft toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste. Rinse with water after acidic foods. See a dentist for bonding or veneers if severe. Treat underlying reflux.
precautions: Use a straw to reduce contact with teeth
Wait 30 minutes after eating acidic foods before brushing
Use fluoride rinses to strengthen enamel
If you have acid reflux, seek treatment

symptoms: sharp, short pain in response to hot, cold, sweet, or sour stimuli
guidance: Use desensitising toothpaste (with potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride). Apply with a soft brush. Avoid acidic foods. If persistent, your dentist can apply fluoride varnish or bonding. Treat any underlying cause (gum recession, enamel loss).
precautions: Avoid acidic foods that worsen sensitivity
If sensitivity persists, see a dentist

guidance: Bruxism can be caused by stress, anxiety, or sleep disorders. Treatment: custom‑made night guard to protect teeth. Stress management, relaxation techniques, and avoiding caffeine before bed. Severe cases may need Botox or splints. Free dental advice at government hospitals.
precautions: Wear a night guard as prescribed
Avoid caffeine and alcohol before sleep
If you have sleep apnea, treat it
Regular dental checkups to monitor wear

guidance: Malocclusion can be corrected with orthodontic treatment (braces or aligners). Early intervention (age 7–12) improves outcomes. Free orthodontic treatment is available at some government dental colleges. In severe cases, surgery may be needed.
precautions: If you have crooked teeth, see an orthodontist
Maintain good oral hygiene (crowded teeth trap plaque)
Wear retainers after braces to prevent relapse
If you have jaw pain, mention it

symptoms: pain or swelling in the back of the jaw
guidance: Impacted wisdom teeth may need removal (extraction) if they cause pain, infection, or damage to adjacent teeth. Surgery is done by an oral surgeon. Free surgery is available at government hospitals. If asymptomatic, they may be monitored.
precautions: If you have pain in the back of your jaw, see a dentist
If you have swelling, apply cold packs
If surgery is planned, follow pre‑ and post‑op instructions

symptoms: pain, swelling, and redness around a partially erupted wisdom tooth
guidance: Pericoronitis is an infection of the gum flap covering a partially erupted tooth. Treatment: cleaning, irrigating the area, antibiotics, and sometimes extraction. Warm salt water rinses and pain relief. If recurrent, remove the tooth. Free emergency care.
precautions: Rinse with warm salt water several times a day
If you have swelling, see a dentist

guidance: Extrinsic stains can be removed with professional cleaning or whitening toothpaste. Intrinsic stains (from tetracycline, fluorosis, trauma) may need bleaching, veneers, or crowns. Consult a dentist. Home whitening kits may help for mild stains.
precautions: Avoid excessive coffee, tea, and red wine
If you have fluorosis, discuss management

category: Dental Erosion from Bulimia / Acid Reflux
symptoms: smooth, shiny, or flattened tooth surfaces
enamel loss on the palatal surfaces of front teeth
guidance: Erosion is caused by stomach acid. If due to bulimia, seek psychological help. If reflux, treat with PPIs. Use fluoride rinses and avoid brushing immediately after vomiting (rinse with water first). See a dentist for restorative options.
precautions: Rinse with water after vomiting, do not brush
If you have reflux, avoid lying down after meals
See a dentist for bonding to protect eroded areas

symptoms: white patches or plaques in the mouth that cannot be scraped off
commonly on cheeks, tongue, floor of mouth
guidance: Leukoplakia is a precancerous lesion. Biopsy is recommended to rule out dysplasia. If benign, monitor. Stop tobacco and alcohol. If dysplastic, surgical excision. Free oral cancer screening at government hospitals. Do not ignore.
precautions: If you have a white patch >2 weeks, see a dentist

symptoms: bright red, velvety patch in the mouth
most common on floor of mouth, soft palate
guidance: Erythroplakia has a higher risk of malignancy than leukoplakia. Urgent biopsy is required. Stop tobacco and alcohol. If dysplastic or malignant, surgical excision. Free treatment at government hospitals. Do not delay.

symptoms: non‑healing ulcer or growth in the mouth
guidance: Oral cancer is common in India due to tobacco use. Immediate biopsy and referral to an oncologist. Treatment: surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy – free under PMJAY. Prevention: avoid tobacco and alcohol. Regular oral screening.
precautions: If you have an ulcer >2 weeks, seek biopsy
If you have a lump in the neck, get evaluated

symptoms: burning sensation (especially on eating spicy food)
guidance: OSMF is strongly associated with areca nut (pan, gutkha) chewing. Treatment: stop the habit. Physiotherapy (jaw opening exercises), corticosteroids, and antioxidants. If severe, surgery may be needed. Regular monitoring for malignant transformation. Free care at government hospitals.
precautions: Stop areca nut, pan, and tobacco
If you have difficulty opening your mouth, see a dentist

symptoms: white, lacy (reticular) patches on the buccal mucosa, gums, or tongue
burning sensation, especially with spicy foods
guidance: Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition. Erosive forms need treatment with topical corticosteroids or immunosuppressants. Regular monitoring – there is a small risk of malignant transformation. Avoid triggers (stress, spicy foods, alcohol). Free care at dermatology/dental departments.
precautions: If you have erosive lichen planus, see a specialist regularly

symptoms: painful, flaccid blisters and erosions on the oral mucosa
guidance: Oral pemphigus is a serious autoimmune condition requiring systemic corticosteroids and immunosuppressants (azathioprine, rituximab). Prompt diagnosis by biopsy and immunofluorescence. Free rituximab at some government centres. Dental care is supportive.
precautions: Do not delay – can be fatal
If you have persistent oral ulcers, see a dermatologist

symptoms: chronic, painful blisters and erosions in the mouth
may affect eyes, skin, or genitals
positive biopsy with linear IgG at basement membrane
guidance: Treatment: topical or systemic corticosteroids, and sometimes dapsone or immunosuppressants. Ocular involvement needs ophthalmology referral. Good oral hygiene with soft brushing. Free care at dermatology departments.
precautions: If you have oral blisters, see a doctor
If you have eye symptoms, see an ophthalmologist

symptoms: smooth, red, irregular patches on the tongue surface
may be asymptomatic or slightly sensitive to spicy foods
guidance: Geographic tongue is a benign condition. No treatment needed if asymptomatic. Avoid irritating foods if sensitive. Reassurance. If you have pain, topical anesthetics may help. Not associated with cancer.
precautions: If sensitive, avoid spicy, acidic, or hot foods
If you have pain, see a dentist

symptoms: deep grooves or fissures on the dorsal surface of the tongue
may accumulate food debris leading to bad breath or irritation
guidance: Fissured tongue is benign. Keep the tongue clean by brushing or scraping it gently. If debris accumulates, clean regularly. No treatment needed. If painful, rule out infection.
precautions: Clean the tongue with a scraper
If you have bad breath, clean the grooves
If you have pain, see a dentist

symptoms: black, brown, or yellow discolouration of the tongue
usually associated with poor oral hygiene, smoking, or antibiotics
guidance: Hairy tongue is benign. Improve oral hygiene: brush the tongue, use a scraper. Stop smoking. If caused by antibiotics, it usually resolves after stopping. If persistent, see a dentist.
precautions: If discolouration persists, see a dentist

symptoms: white, curd‑like patches on the tongue, inner cheeks, or palate
cracking at the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis)
guidance: Oral thrush is caused by Candida. Treatment: antifungal lozenges (clotrimazole, nystatin) or oral fluconazole. Clean dentures and treat underlying diabetes. Avoid sugary foods. Free antifungals at government hospitals.
precautions: Clean dentures and soak in antifungal solution
If you have diabetes, control blood sugar
If you have dry mouth, stay hydrated

category: Angular Cheilitis (Cracked Corners of the Mouth)
symptoms: red, cracked, or scaly skin at the corners of the mouth
may be caused by fungal (Candida) or bacterial infection, nutritional deficiency (riboflavin, iron), or ill‑fitting dentures
guidance: Treat with antifungal/antibiotic cream (e.g., clotrimazole + hydrocortisone). If due to nutritional deficiency, supplement with B vitamins and iron. Keep the area dry. Use lip balm. If dentures are the cause, adjust them.
precautions: Keep the corners of the mouth dry
If you have dentures, ensure they fit well
Do not lick the corners – worsens

symptoms: tingling or burning sensation before eruption
clusters of small, painful blisters on the lips or around the mouth
often triggered by fever, sun, stress
guidance: Apply topical acyclovir or penciclovir at the first sign to reduce duration. Oral antivirals (acyclovir) for frequent recurrences. Use lip balm with SPF. Avoid sharing utensils. If you have a cold sore, avoid contact with immunocompromised.
precautions: Do not share lip products or utensils
If you have a weakened immune system, seek treatment
Wash hands after touching the sore

symptoms: vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution (often maxillary or mandibular)
may involve the oral mucosa, leading to ulcers
guidance: Antiviral (acyclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset. Pain management (gabapentin, pregabalin). If oral, use topical anesthetics and soft diet. Free antivirals. Vaccination prevents shingles.
precautions: If you have a rash on the face, see a doctor
If you have severe pain, treat it

symptoms: painful, round, shallow ulcers with a yellow‑grey centre and red halo
usually on the inner lips, cheeks, or tongue
triggered by stress, trauma, or certain foods
guidance: Most resolve in 1–2 weeks. Use topical anesthetics, corticosteroids (triamcinolone), or protective pastes. Avoid spicy, acidic, or rough foods. Stress management. If frequent, check for nutritional deficiencies (B12, folate, iron). Free dental care.
precautions: Apply topical treatments at the first sign
If you have frequent ulcers, see a doctor

symptoms: soft, painless, fluid‑filled swelling on the inner lip, floor of mouth, or buccal mucosa
often caused by trauma or blocked salivary gland
guidance: Small mucoceles may resolve spontaneously. If persistent or recurrent, surgical excision is needed. Do not attempt to pop it. Free minor surgery at government hospitals. Reassurance.
precautions: If you have a cyst, do not try to burst it
If it recurs, surgery may be needed

symptoms: pain and swelling in the submandibular or parotid area, especially during meals
guidance: Stones can block salivary flow. Treatment: massage, hydration, sour candies to stimulate saliva. If persistent, surgical removal (sialolithotomy) or sialendoscopy. Free ENT/dental care. If infection, antibiotics.
precautions: Suck on lemon drops to stimulate saliva
If you have recurrent swelling, see a dentist
If you have fever, seek antibiotics

symptoms: painful swelling of the salivary gland (parotid or submandibular)
guidance: Treatment: antibiotics (penicillin or cephalexin), hydration, massage, and warm compresses. If an abscess forms, surgical drainage. Free care at government hospitals. Prevention: good oral hygiene and hydration.
precautions: If you have swelling and fever, see a doctor
If you have a stone, treat it

symptoms: dry, sticky feeling in the mouth
guidance: Common causes: antihistamines, decongestants, diuretics, antidepressants. Management: sip water frequently, use sugar‑free lozenges, artificial saliva, avoid caffeine/alcohol. If medication is the cause, discuss alternatives. Good oral hygiene is essential.
precautions: Use artificial saliva or moisturising mouthwash
If you have dry mouth, brush and floss carefully
If you have dentures, keep them moist

symptoms: dental caries (due to lack of saliva)
guidance: Sjögren's is an autoimmune disease. Management: saliva substitutes, pilocarpine (to stimulate saliva), fluoride varnishes, and good oral hygiene. Regular dental visits. Treat dry eyes with artificial tears. Free rheumatology care.
precautions: If you have dry eyes, see an ophthalmologist

category: Dental Caries in Children (Early Childhood Caries)
symptoms: white spots or brown cavities on baby teeth (often on upper front teeth)
guidance: Prevention: avoid putting sugary liquids in bottles at bedtime, clean baby's gums, and introduce fluoride toothpaste. If caries develops, fillings or crowns may be needed. Free dental care for children at government hospitals.
precautions: Clean baby's gums with a soft cloth
Once teeth erupt, brush with a tiny amount of fluoride toothpaste
Do not put baby to bed with a bottle
Take your child to the dentist by age 1

symptoms: swelling or bluish‑purple cyst over an erupting tooth (usually a baby molar)
guidance: Teething is a normal process. Use a clean, cool teething ring. Rub the gums with a clean finger. If the cyst is large, a dentist may need to incise it. Paracetamol for pain (as per weight). No aspirin.
precautions: Do not give aspirin to children
If the cyst is large, see a dentist
If fever is high, rule out other causes

symptoms: open bite (front teeth do not meet)
guidance: Most children stop thumb sucking by age 4. If it persists, encourage cessation with positive reinforcement, not punishment. In severe cases, an orthodontist may recommend a habit‑breaking appliance. Free orthodontic consultation.
precautions: Do not punish – encourage positive behaviour
If persistent after age 5, see a dentist
If you have an appliance, follow the orthodontist's advice

guidance: Treat underlying nasal obstruction (allergies, deviated septum). Myofunctional exercises may help. Orthodontic expansion may be needed in children. Early intervention improves facial development. Free ENT/dental care.
precautions: If you have nasal congestion, treat it
If your child mouth‑breathes, see a dentist
If you have sleep apnea, treat it

guidance: Handle the tooth by the crown (not root). Rinse with milk or saline if dirty (do not scrub). Re‑implant if possible, or store in milk. See a dentist immediately – time is critical (ideally within 30 minutes). Do not store in water.
precautions: Store in milk if re‑implantation is not possible
If in doubt, go to the nearest dental emergency

symptoms: visible break or crack in the tooth
guidance: Save any broken pieces. Rinse mouth with water. Apply a cold pack to reduce swelling. See a dentist as soon as possible. If the pulp is exposed, a root canal may be needed. Free emergency care.
precautions: Do not chew on the injured side
If the pulp is exposed, avoid hot/cold

symptoms: tooth pushed in, out, or sideways
guidance: Do not try to push it back. See a dentist immediately. Treatment: repositioning and splinting. If the tooth is intruded, it may need surgical repositioning. Early treatment improves outcomes.
precautions: Do not try to move the tooth yourself
If the tooth is avulsed, follow avulsion protocol

category: Dental Trauma – Soft Tissue Injury (Lips, Cheeks, Tongue)
symptoms: laceration, puncture, or tear of the lip, cheek, or tongue
guidance: Apply pressure with a clean cloth to stop bleeding. Rinse the mouth with salt water. If the wound is deep or involves the lip border, seek medical/dental care. Sutures may be needed. Watch for infection.
precautions: If bleeding does not stop, seek medical care
If the tongue is injured, avoid hot foods
If you have a deep wound, see a doctor

symptoms: pain on opening or closing the mouth
numbness of the lower lip (mandibular fracture)
guidance: This is a maxillofacial emergency – go to the emergency room. Immobilise the jaw with a bandage (if possible). Do not eat or drink. Surgery (wire fixation or plates) may be needed. Free treatment at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have numbness, tell the doctor

guidance: This is a medical emergency. Do not try to close the jaw forcefully. Go to the emergency room – manual reduction is needed. After reduction, use a soft diet and jaw exercises. Avoid wide opening.
precautions: Do not force the jaw closed
After reduction, follow your doctor's advice
Use a soft diet for a few days

symptoms: clicking, popping, or grating sounds in the TMJ
locking of the jaw (open or closed)
guidance: Management: soft diet, avoid extreme jaw movements, apply heat/cold packs, stress reduction, and jaw exercises. Occlusal splints (night guards) may help. If symptoms persist, see a dentist or oral surgeon. Free TMJ treatment at government dental colleges.
precautions: Use a night guard if you grind
If you have pain, apply heat

symptoms: history of respiratory, gastrointestinal, or sinus conditions
guidance: Bad breath can originate from the mouth, nose, sinuses, or stomach. Maintain good oral hygiene, brush the tongue, and stay hydrated. If persistent, see a doctor to rule out sinusitis, GERD, or diabetes. Free dental checkups.

symptoms: chronic burning sensation in the mouth (tongue, lips, palate)
may be worse in the evening
associated with anxiety, nutritional deficiencies, or endocrine disorders
guidance: Treatment: address underlying causes (nutritional deficiencies (B12, folate, iron), diabetes, thyroid, or stress). Use artificial saliva, and avoid spicy foods. Low‑dose antidepressants or gabapentin may help. Free care at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid spicy, acidic, and hot foods
If you have nutritional deficiencies, supplement
If you have diabetes, control it

symptoms: persistent bitter, metallic, or salty taste in the mouth
often associated with medications, infections, or nutritional deficiencies
guidance: Identify and treat the cause: medications, oral infections, sinusitis, or zinc deficiency. Maintain oral hygiene. Use plastic utensils if metallic taste is due to dental metals. Free consultation at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have a sinus infection, treat it
If you have a deficiency (zinc), supplement

symptoms: white spots or streaks on tooth enamel
occurs in children during tooth development (excessive fluoride intake)
guidance: Prevention: avoid excessive fluoride intake in children (use fluoride toothpaste in pea‑sized amounts, monitor water fluoride levels). If fluorosis is mild, bleaching or microabrasion may help. Severe cases need veneers or crowns.
precautions: Check fluoride levels in drinking water
Use low‑fluoride toothpaste for children under 3
If you have fluorosis, discuss cosmetic options

guidance: Management: protective restorations (crowns), desensitising agents, and good oral hygiene. Veneers or full crowns may be needed. Genetic counselling. Free dental care at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have sensitive teeth, use desensitising toothpaste

guidance: Restorative treatment: crowns to protect teeth. Early intervention is key. Manage pain and infection. Genetic counselling. Free dental care.
precautions: If you have a toothache, see a dentist
If you have a family history, consult early

category: Tooth Eruption Problems (Impacted, Delayed, or Supernumerary)
guidance: Radiographs are needed to assess. Treatment: extraction of supernumerary teeth, orthodontic exposure of impacted teeth, or space maintainers. Early intervention (age 7–9) is best. Free orthodontic care at dental colleges.
precautions: If your child's teeth are delayed, see a dentist
If you have pain, seek care

symptoms: one or more upper teeth biting inside the lower teeth
guidance: Early correction (in children) may involve expansion appliances. In adults, braces or aligners. If skeletal, surgery may be needed. Free orthodontic evaluation at government dental colleges.
precautions: If you have a crossbite, see an orthodontist
Early treatment in children is easier
If you have jaw pain, mention it

symptoms: front teeth do not touch when biting
guidance: Causes: thumb sucking, tongue thrusting, or skeletal. Treatment: habit modification, orthodontic appliances (cribs), or braces. In severe cases, surgery. Early intervention is key.
precautions: If you have an open bite, see an orthodontist
If you have surgery, follow pre‑op instructions

symptoms: upper front teeth significantly overlap the lower front teeth
gum trauma behind upper front teeth
guidance: Treatment: orthodontic braces to correct. In severe cases, surgery. Treat with functional appliances in children. Free orthodontic care at government dental colleges.
precautions: If you have a deep bite, see an orthodontist
If you have jaw pain, mention it

symptoms: lower teeth protrude in front of upper teeth
guidance: Treatment: orthodontic appliances (facemask) in children; braces and sometimes surgery in adults. Early treatment (age 7–10) may reduce severity. Free orthodontic consultation.
precautions: If you have an underbite, see an orthodontist
If you have pain, mention it

symptoms: used after premature loss of primary teeth to maintain space for permanent teeth
guidance: If a primary tooth is lost early, a space maintainer (band/loop, crown) prevents adjacent teeth from drifting. This avoids future crowding. Appliance is cemented by a dentist and should be checked regularly.
precautions: If your child loses a tooth early, see a dentist
If the appliance is loose, see a dentist

symptoms: plastic coating applied to the chewing surfaces of molars to prevent decay
guidance: Sealants are recommended for children and adolescents (and high‑caries adults). They are placed on permanent molars soon after eruption. The procedure is quick and painless. Free sealants in government school dental programs.
precautions: If you have deep grooves, ask about sealants
Sealants are not a substitute for brushing
If a sealant falls off, get it replaced
Good for children – prevents up to 80% of cavities

symptoms: varnish, gel, or foam applied to teeth to prevent decay and remineralise early lesions
guidance: Fluoride varnish is applied every 3–6 months for children and high‑risk adults. It is quick and painless. Do not eat or drink for 30 minutes after application. Free at government dental clinics.
precautions: Get fluoride varnish if you have a high cavity risk
Avoid eating or drinking for 30 minutes
If you have fluorosis, use with caution

guidance: Dental X‑rays are safe with proper shielding (lead apron and thyroid collar). They help detect cavities, bone loss, and impacted teeth. Avoid X‑rays in pregnancy unless necessary. Government dental clinics provide affordable X‑rays.
precautions: If you are pregnant, inform the dentist
Use lead apron and thyroid shield
If you have a child, use child‑sized films

category: Oral Hygiene Aids – Toothbrush, Floss, Interdental Brushes
guidance: Use a soft‑bristled toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste. Replace the brush every 3 months. Floss daily to clean between teeth. Interdental brushes are good for wider gaps. Mouthwash is optional. Free toothbrushes are distributed in some government programs.
precautions: Rinse and dry the brush after use
Do not use a hard brush – it damages gums
If you have braces, use special floss threaders

guidance: Brush with a soft brush at a 45° angle to the gumline. Use short, gentle circular motions. Brush all surfaces (outer, inner, and chewing). Brush for 2 minutes twice daily. Do not scrub too hard. Replace the brush every 3 months.
precautions: Use gentle pressure – not vigorous scrubbing
If you have sensitivity, use a soft brush

category: Interdental Cleaning – Flossing and Water Flossers
guidance: Floss daily – break off 18 inches, wrap around fingers, guide between teeth using a gentle sawing motion, curve around each tooth, and go below the gumline. Water flossers (irrigators) are useful for braces or bridges.
precautions: Do not snap floss against gums
If you have bleeding, floss gently – it may improve with time
Use a floss holder if you have arthritis
Water flossers are not a substitute for flossing

guidance: Clean the tongue daily with a tongue scraper or the back of the toothbrush. This removes bacteria, reduces bad breath, and improves taste. Start from the back and move forward. Rinse after each stroke.
precautions: Do not scrape too hard – can damage taste buds
Rinse the scraper after each use
If you have a fissured tongue, clean carefully
If you have thrush, cleaning helps

guidance: Eat a balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein. Limit sugar (sweets, soda, juice) – sugar feeds cavity‑causing bacteria. Calcium and vitamin D are important for teeth. Drink fluoridated water.
precautions: Eat cheese or nuts to neutralise acid

guidance: Wear a mouthguard during contact sports (football, hockey, boxing, martial arts) to protect teeth and jaws. Custom‑made mouthguards from a dentist are best. Boil‑and‑bite types are available over‑the‑counter.
precautions: Wear a mouthguard when playing sports
If you have braces, use a special mouthguard

guidance: Dental anxiety is common. Communicate your fears with the dentist. Use relaxation techniques (deep breathing). Nitrous oxide (laughing gas) or sedation dentistry may be available. Free counselling at some dental centres.
precautions: Tell your dentist about your anxiety
Start with a simple checkup to build trust
If you have a phobia, ask about sedation options

guidance: Clean dentures daily with a soft brush and mild soap (not toothpaste). Remove them at night and soak in water or cleaning solution. Massage the gums. Visit the dentist for adjustments. Free denture care at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have sore spots, see a dentist
Clean your gums with a soft brush

guidance: Dental implants need regular care: brush around the implant, use a water flosser, and have regular professional checkups. Avoid chewing on hard objects. If you have pain or mobility, see a dentist.
precautions: Visit your dentist twice a year
If you have swelling or pain, see a dentist

guidance: Brush after every meal, using an interdental brush and floss threaders. Avoid hard, sticky, and sugary foods. Wear elastics as prescribed. Regular orthodontic adjustments. Free care at government dental colleges.
precautions: Avoid sticky and hard foods (caramel, nuts, popcorn)

category: Oral Manifestations of Diabetes – Gingivitis, Caries, Thrush
symptoms: poor wound healing after dental procedures
guidance: Good glycaemic control improves oral health. Brush and floss regularly. Visit the dentist every 6 months. Treat thrush promptly. If you have periodontal disease, inform your endocrinologist. Free dental care.
precautions: If you have dry mouth, stay hydrated
If you have thrush, treat it

guidance: Treat infections aggressively. Use antifungal, antiviral, and antiretroviral therapy. Maintain good oral hygiene. Regular dental follow‑up. Free ART and dental care under NACO.
precautions: If you have HIV, see a dentist regularly

category: Oral Manifestations of Blood Disorders (Anemia, Leukemia)
symptoms: decreased immunity leading to oral infections
guidance: Treat the underlying blood disorder. Maintain meticulous oral hygiene. Avoid trauma to gums. Bleeding risk – inform dentist before procedures. Free haematology and dental care.
precautions: If you have anaemia, take iron supplements
If you have a bleeding disorder, inform your dentist
If you have ulcers, see a doctor

symptoms: Vitamin C deficiency – bleeding gums, loose teeth
Vitamin D deficiency – delayed eruption, enamel defects
guidance: Supplement the deficient vitamin. Eat a balanced diet. Treat symptoms with topical agents. See a doctor for diagnosis. Free supplementation at government health centres.
precautions: If you have glossitis, check B vitamins
If you have bleeding gums, check vitamin C
If you have angular cheilitis, check B2 and iron
If you have a deficiency, supplement

symptoms: swollen, red, bleeding gums during pregnancy
guidance: Brush gently with a soft brush, floss daily, and use a mild mouthwash. Visit the dentist – professional cleaning is safe during pregnancy. Control plaque. Usually resolves after delivery. Free prenatal dental care.
precautions: Do not avoid dental visits – they are safe
If you have a growth, see a dentist
If you have nausea, rinse with water after vomiting

guidance: Routine dental care is safe during pregnancy. Inform your dentist of your pregnancy. Elective procedures should be avoided in the first trimester and late third trimester. Local anaesthetics (lidocaine) are safe. Avoid X‑rays unless necessary.
precautions: Inform your dentist if you are pregnant
Delay elective treatment until after delivery
If you have a dental emergency, don't delay

symptoms: tooth loss, dry mouth, root caries
guidance: Elderly need regular dental visits. Manage dry mouth with saliva substitutes. Prevent root caries with fluoride. Check dentures for fit. Screen for oral cancer. Free geriatric dental care at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have dry mouth, use artificial saliva
If you have difficulty chewing, see a dentist

symptoms: gingival hyperplasia (e.g., from phenytoin, calcium channel blockers)
guidance: Review medications with your doctor and dentist. Use saliva substitutes and fluoride. Maintain good hygiene. If you have gum overgrowth, discuss alternative medications. Free dental care.
precautions: If you have dry mouth, drink water often
If you have gum overgrowth, see a dentist

guidance: Ill‑fitting dentures need adjustments or relining. Do not use over‑the‑counter adhesives as a long‑term solution. See a dentist for proper fitting. Free denture services at government hospitals.
precautions: Do not try to adjust dentures yourself
If you have sore spots, see a dentist

symptoms: cavities on the root surfaces of teeth (exposed due to gum recession)
sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet
guidance: Use fluoride toothpaste and mouthwash. Reduce sugar intake. Treat with fillings. If deep, root canal. Prevention: good oral hygiene and fluoride. Free dental care.
precautions: If you have gum recession, use fluoride
Brush gently to avoid worsening recession
If you have sensitivity, use desensitising toothpaste

symptoms: take longer to heal (up to 6 weeks)
guidance: Topical corticosteroids (triamcinolone) and protective pastes. In severe cases, systemic corticosteroids or colchicine. Check for nutritional deficiencies. Avoid trauma. Free dental care.
precautions: If you have frequent major ulcers, see a doctor
If you have a fever, rule out other causes

symptoms: resemble herpes but are not herpes (aphthous variant)
guidance: Treat with topical corticosteroids and analgesics. Usually benign. If persistent, rule out underlying systemic disease. Free care.
precautions: If you have many ulcers, see a doctor
If you have a fever, rule out infection

symptoms: white, reticular, or erosive lesions in the mouth
guidance: Identify and stop the offending medication (with your doctor's advice). Use topical corticosteroids. Biopsy if persistent. Free dermatology/dental care.
precautions: If you have lichenoid lesions, review your medications
Do not stop medication without consulting
If you have pain, see a dentist

guidance: Systemic corticosteroids, dapsone, or immunosuppressants. Ocular involvement needs ophthalmology. Regular monitoring. Free care.
precautions: If you have oral blisters, see a dermatologist

category: Cleft Lip and Palate – Dental Care
symptoms: cleft lip and/or palate present at birth
guidance: Multidisciplinary care: surgery, orthodontics, speech therapy. Dental care includes orthodontic treatment and prosthetics. Free treatment under government schemes. Regular dental follow‑up.
precautions: If you have a cleft, see a paediatric dentist
If you have speech issues, see a speech therapist

guidance: If breastfeeding is affected, frenotomy (clip) may be done. For older children, if speech is affected, a frenectomy may be needed. Free procedure at government hospitals.
precautions: If your baby has trouble latching, see a doctor
If you have speech issues, see a dentist

category: Mouth Breathing – Dry Mouth and Dental Health
guidance: Treat the cause (allergies, deviated septum). Use a humidifier, drink water, and use saliva substitutes. Regular dental checkups. Free ENT and dental care.
precautions: If you mouth‑breathe, treat nasal obstruction
If you have sleep apnea, treat it

guidance: Orthodontic expansion can improve airway. Oral appliances (mandibular advancement devices) are used for mild sleep apnea. Treat with CPAP if needed. Free orthodontic and sleep clinics.
precautions: If you have sleep apnea, get evaluated
If you have crowded teeth, see an orthodontist
Follow up with a sleep specialist

symptoms: periodontitis is a risk factor for heart disease
no direct oral symptoms, but gum disease increases systemic inflammation
guidance: Maintain good oral hygiene to reduce systemic inflammation. If you have heart disease, inform your dentist before procedures (need antibiotic prophylaxis). Free dental and cardiac care.
precautions: If you have heart disease, tell your dentist
If you have gum disease, treat it
If you are on blood thinners, inform your dentist

symptoms: poorly controlled diabetes worsens periodontal disease
guidance: Good oral hygiene improves blood sugar control. Treat periodontal disease aggressively. Visit the dentist regularly. Free diabetes and dental care.
precautions: If you have bleeding gums, see a dentist
If you have dry mouth, stay hydrated

category: Oral Health and Respiratory Infections (Aspiration Pneumonia)
symptoms: poor oral hygiene can lead to aspiration of oral bacteria
especially in elderly or nursing home residents
guidance: Good oral care in elderly and disabled reduces pneumonia risk. Daily brushing, denture cleaning, and oral swabbing. Free geriatric dental care.
precautions: If you care for an elderly person, provide oral hygiene
If you have a cough, see a doctor

category: Oral Health and Chronic Kidney Disease
symptoms: dry mouth, altered taste, bad breath
guidance: Maintain oral hygiene. Treat gum disease – it may affect kidney function. If on dialysis, schedule dental visits on non‑dialysis days. Free dental and nephrology care.
precautions: If you have CKD, see a dentist regularly
If you have dry mouth, stay hydrated
If you have gum disease, treat it
Inform your dentist about your kidney function

symptoms: associated with bisphosphonate use (risk of osteonecrosis)
guidance: If you are on bisphosphonates, inform your dentist – risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw after extractions. Maintain good hygiene. Free osteoporosis screening.
precautions: If you are on bisphosphonates, tell your dentist
If you have loose teeth, see a dentist

symptoms: periodontitis is more common in RA
guidance: Treat periodontal disease – it may improve RA symptoms. Use warm compresses for TMJ. Soft diet. Free rheumatology and dental care.
precautions: If you have RA, see a dentist regularly
If you have jaw pain, use warm compresses
If you have dry mouth, stay hydrated
If you have TMJ, see a specialist

guidance: Patients with certain heart conditions (valvular disease, prosthetic valves, congenital heart disease) need antibiotics before dental procedures to prevent infective endocarditis. Follow AHA guidelines. Free antibiotics at government hospitals.
precautions: If you have a heart condition, inform your dentist
Take antibiotics as prescribed before procedures
Do not skip – can be life‑saving
If you have a prosthetic joint, discuss prophylaxis
Keep a list of your conditions

symptoms: toothache, swelling, bleeding, trauma, loose tooth, abscess
guidance: For pain, take paracetamol. For swelling, apply cold pack. For bleeding, apply pressure. Do not place aspirin on the tooth – burns the gum. See a dentist as soon as possible. Free emergency dental care.
precautions: Do not place aspirin on the gum
If you have swelling, see a dentist
If you have a knocked‑out tooth, see a dentist within 30 minutes
Do not delay – infections can spread

category: Dental Care in Developing Countries – Simple Measures
guidance: Use fluoridated toothpaste. Chew sugar‑free gum after meals. Avoid sticky sweets. Drink water. Visit a dentist if possible. Use traditional chewing sticks (miswak) with caution – they can help but not replace brushing. Free dental checkups at health camps.
precautions: If you use miswak, use it with toothpaste

guidance: Community dental health education can prevent most oral diseases. Brush twice, floss, and limit sugar. Schools should teach oral hygiene. Government has school dental health programs. Participate and spread awareness.
precautions: If you have a problem, seek early care
